subject: Business
title: Compound Interest: The Eighth Wonder
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Compound Interest: The Eighth Wonder.

hook.text: Invest $1,000 at 10% annually. In 30 years it becomes $17,449 — without adding a single dollar.

buildup.text: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Each year, the base grows larger.

discovery.text: The Rule of 72: divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

twist.text: Compound interest works against you too. Credit card debt at 24% doubles in just three years.

climax.text: Warren Buffett made 99% of his wealth after age 50. Compounding rewards patience above all else.

punchline.text: Time is the ingredient. Compound interest is the recipe.

quiz.question: Using the Rule of 72, how long does it take money to double at 8% annual interest?

details.summary: Compound interest earns returns on both your original investment and all previously accumulated interest, creating exponential growth over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called it the eighth wonder of the world because the effect accelerates dramatically with time.
details.whyItMatters: Compound interest is the most powerful force in personal finance. Starting early matters enormously because each additional year of compounding multiplies the final result far more than adding extra money later.
takeaways: Compounding earns interest on interest, creating exponential growth
Time is the critical variable that makes compounding extraordinarily powerful
The Rule of 72 estimates years to double by dividing 72 by the interest rate

faq.question: How does the Rule of 72 work in practice?
faq.answer: Divide 72 by the annual return rate. At 8 percent returns, your money doubles in approximately 9 years. At 6 percent, it takes about 12 years. This mental shortcut helps you quickly estimate how investments grow without a calculator.

faq.question: Why does starting to invest early matter so much?
faq.answer: Someone investing 200 dollars monthly from age 25 to 65 at 8 percent accumulates roughly 700,000 dollars. Starting at 35 yields only about 300,000 dollars. Those first 10 years contribute almost half the total due to compounding over the longest period.
